strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored task: reinforcement learning for chart-to-code generation, where structured outputs and information-dense visual inputs make SFT alone insufficient.
Constructs a large-scale training corpus of 3M chart-code pairs from real-world arXiv tables with multi-stage filtering, enabling a systematic study of SFT data scaling.
Systematically identifies and quantifies the SFT performance plateau across multiple data scales, providing useful empirical evidence for the community.
Proposes MSRL, a well-motivated multi-granularity reward design combining rule-based textual rewards with render-and-compare visual rewards, plus a two-stage curriculum for stability.
Reports strong empirical results: new SOTA among open-source models on ChartMimic and ReachQA, outperforming prior chart-specific models and rivaling GPT-4o on many metrics.
Includes useful ablations on SFT vs. RL, reward combinations, and one-stage vs. two-stage RL, as well as qualitative visual comparisons.
The paper is generally clearly written and well structured, with a coherent pipeline from data construction to RL training and evaluation.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the main components—rule-based code rewards, render-and-compare visual feedback, GRPO, and curriculum RL—are largely known, so the contribution is more an effective combination than a fundamentally new algorithm.

Evaluation is limited to two benchmarks and lacks error bars or statistical significance testing; several claimed gains, especially over a strong textual-only RL baseline, are marginal (e.g., Table 5 high-level 83.83 vs. 82.69).

Reward definition is technically inconsistent: the paper states the textual reward includes execution correctness, but Equation 1 introduces a separate R_exec term without clearly defining the final reward composition and normalization.

The visual reward uses Qwen2.5-VL-72B, the same model family as the 7B policy, with no human validation or reward-hacking analysis; it is unclear whether the visual evaluator’s scores reliably reflect true chart fidelity.
Reproducibility is limited: the dataset, model, and code are not released, and training relies on proprietary APIs (Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-4.1-mini) and substantial H800 GPU resources.
The SFT plateau study is restricted to one 7B model and one training epoch, so the plateau conclusion may not generalize across model sizes, objectives, or hyperparameters.

Data quality is not fully audited: the corpus is generated using LLM-generated code from arXiv tables, with automatic filtering but no reported human inspection of noise, bias, or benchmark contamination.
The paper overstates claims such as “first/largest” corpus and “significantly breaks the SFT plateau” without sufficient statistical evidence or broader validation.

strengths: Constructs a large-scale chart-to-code corpus (3M pairs) using real-world arXiv tables and a multi-stage generation/filtering pipeline, which could be a useful resource if released.
Provides an empirical study of SFT data scaling and identifies a performance plateau for chart-to-code generation, offering a useful diagnostic observation.

Proposes MSRL, combining rule-based textual rewards and MLLM-based visual rewards with a two-stage RL curriculum, and reports strong results on ChartMimic and ReachQA, outperforming prior open-source chart-specific models and approaching proprietary models.
Includes ablations over reward types and RL stages, which helps clarify the contribution of textual vs. visual rewards and two-stage training.
The application domain is relevant and practically important for multimodal structured generation.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the method largely combines existing ingredients (SFT, GRPO, rule-based rewards, MLLM-as-judge visual rewards, two-stage curriculum) rather than introducing a fundamentally new technique. The core finding of an SFT plateau is empirical but demonstrated only for one base model and one constructed dataset.

Missing important baselines: recent RL-based chart/reasoning models mentioned in related work, such as Chart-R1 and BigCharts-R1, are not compared. There is also no comparison to DPO/preference-based methods despite the paper motivating their limitations. Additional benchmarks such as Plot2Code and ChartX are omitted.

Evaluation lacks statistical rigor: no error bars, significance tests, or multiple random seeds are reported. Several ablation gains are very small (e.g., two-stage textual then textual+visual vs. single-stage textual+visual), so the central claims about visual rewards and two-stage RL are not strongly supported and could be noise.

Potential data contamination is not addressed. The training corpus is built from arXiv papers, and ChartMimic may draw from similar arXiv charts. Without explicit overlap analysis, reported gains on ChartMimic may be inflated by train/test leakage.

Reward design and technical details are underspecified. Code normalization, layout matching, soft value matching, and the exact five textual reward components are not described sufficiently. Reward weights appear arbitrary and are not sensitivity-tested. Equation 1 also creates confusion about whether execution reward is part of textual reward or separate.

The visual reward uses Qwen2.5-VL-72B, from the same model family as the policy, without validating its reliability or correlation with human judgment. This risks reward hacking/bias. Omitting KL divergence and training for only "one episode" is unusual and may cause instability, yet no stability analysis is provided.

Reproducibility and availability are poor: no clear plan to release the 3M corpus, curated 33k RL set, code, or model weights. The pipeline relies on proprietary APIs (Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-4.1-mini) and expensive 24-GPU training, making reproduction difficult.

Presentation and clarity issues: citation inconsistencies (e.g., Chen et al., Kantharaj et al.), reference formatting problems, and incomplete implementation details. There is no limitations section, broader impact discussion, or ethical/licensing consideration for arXiv-derived data.

Claims are stronger than the evidence: e.g., "significantly outperforms all methods in chart domain" is not fully supported by per-metric low-level results vs. GPT-4o (e.g., Text and Type are lower on ChartMimic). The SFT plateau conclusion is overgeneralized from a single model/dataset and may reflect data quality or training recipe rather than an inherent SFT limit.

strengths: Constructs a large-scale chart-to-code corpus (3M pairs) using real arXiv tables, with a two-stage generation/filtering pipeline, which is a valuable resource and enables the SFT scaling study.
Provides a concrete empirical demonstration of an SFT plateau on chart-to-code generation across data scales, motivating the RL contribution.

Proposes MSRL with multi-granularity textual and visual rewards; the rule-based textual reward and render-and-compare visual reward are sensible and target complementary aspects of code and chart fidelity.
Two-stage RL curriculum (textual-only then textual+visual) is shown to stabilize training and yield best results in ablation (Table 5).
Achieves SOTA on ChartMimic and ReachQA among open-source MLLMs and is competitive with GPT-4o; gains are consistent across execution, low-level, and high-level metrics.
Includes useful ablations (SFT vs. RL, reward components, two-stage design) and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: it combines existing ideas (rule-based RLVR rewards, MLLM-as-judge visual rewards, GRPO, two-stage curricula) for chart-to-code; the main new component is the task-specific reward design and dataset.

Reproducibility is insufficiently supported: the paper does not state whether the 3M dataset, curated RL data, code, or reward-model prompts/evaluator details will be released, and key reward normalization/scoring details are omitted.

The visual reward uses Qwen2.5-VL-72B, the same model family as the 7B policy, which raises potential self-reward/evaluator-bias concerns; no reliability analysis or human correlation of the MLLM judge is provided.
Missing comparisons to recent chart-specific RL methods such as Chart-R1 and BigCharts-R1, which are discussed in related work but not included as baselines, weakening the SOTA claim.

Data split and scaling details have inconsistencies: 3M pairs are described, but SFT uses 2.8M and RL uses 33k, with the remaining data unaccounted for; the Figure 1/SFT scales are also not fully aligned with the text.

The SFT plateau is demonstrated only for this data/model recipe; the paper’s broader claim that SFT itself hits a fundamental plateau is somewhat overclaimed without deeper analysis of data quality, diversity, or model capacity.
No limitations/ethical discussion (e.g., arXiv table licensing, code execution safety, dataset release) is provided.

strengths: The paper constructs a large-scale chart-to-code corpus (about 2.8M SFT and 33K RL pairs) from real-world arXiv tables, which is a substantial resource for the community and addresses the limited scale/diversity of prior synthetic datasets.
It systematically studies SFT data scaling and empirically identifies a performance plateau, providing useful evidence that simply increasing SFT data eventually yields diminishing returns.

The proposed MSRL method combines rule-based textual rewards with an MLLM-based visual reward and a two-stage curriculum, showing a practical way to optimize both fine-grained code details and global chart fidelity.

The experimental evaluation is extensive: it includes two benchmarks, comparisons with open-source and proprietary models, ablations on reward design, visual evaluator choice, RL optimizer, and generalization tests to unseen Seaborn/Plotly libraries.
The paper achieves strong empirical results, including SOTA among open-source models on ChartMimic and ReachQA and performance competitive with or superior to GPT-4o on several metrics.
Reproducibility is partly supported through code, prompt templates, and training details, which helps other researchers build on the method.
weaknesses: Potential benchmark contamination is not fully ruled out: the training corpus is built from arXiv papers published in 2023 and earlier, but ChartMimic/ReachQA may also draw from similar sources; the paper does not provide a thorough deduplication or contamination analysis against all evaluation benchmarks.

The claimed realistic data source refers mainly to the underlying tabular data, but chart images and code are still synthetically generated by an LLM and rendered with Matplotlib; this may limit visual diversity and realism relative to real chart screenshots.

The visual reward relies on an MLLM judge, and benchmark high-level metrics may also depend on MLLM-based evaluation; this raises concerns about circularity or reward hacking, and human validation is limited to small filtering/evaluator-choice studies rather than final model outputs.

Novelty is moderate: multi-granularity rewards combining rule-based and model-based feedback, as well as two-stage RL, are intuitive extensions of existing RLVR/GRPO approaches rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic contribution.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the full dataset is not clearly released, the code normalization and textual reward implementation are not described in sufficient detail, and the data-generation pipeline depends on proprietary LLMs, making exact replication difficult.

Some claims are overstated: the abstract says 3M chart-code pairs while the appendix totals about 2.89M, and the paper calls the corpus 'first large-scale' though prior large-scale chart datasets exist; the two-stage RL is not always superior to visual-only reward in the reported ablation.

The SFT plateau analysis is based on a single base model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) and a fixed training recipe, so it is unclear whether the plateau and MSRL conclusions generalize to other model families or scales.

Statistical rigor is limited: there are no confidence intervals or significance tests, and the OOD generalization results use small test sets, which makes it difficult to assess the robustness of the reported gains.

strengths: Constructs the largest chart-to-code training corpus to date (3M pairs) by leveraging real-world tables from arXiv papers, which improves chart diversity and realism over purely synthetic datasets.
Provides a systematic empirical study of SFT data scaling, identifying a performance plateau after roughly 2M samples, which is a useful analysis for the community.
Proposes a reasonable two-stage RL strategy with multi-granularity rewards: rule-based textual rewards for code correctness and MLLM-based visual rewards for rendered chart fidelity.
Reports strong empirical results on ChartMimic and ReachQA, achieving state-of-the-art performance among open-source models and competitive results against proprietary models such as GPT-4o.
Includes extensive ablations on SFT/RL interplay, reward types, visual evaluator choice, GRPO vs. DPO, dataset comparison, and generalization to Seaborn/Plotly.
Provides implementation details, prompt templates, and supplementary training code, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core method is largely an application of existing RLVR/GRPO ideas to chart-to-code generation; the multi-granularity reward design is intuitive but not technically novel.

The SFT plateau claim is based on a single base model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) and one dataset; without multiple models, seeds, or statistical tests, the plateau may reflect model/training specifics rather than a general property of SFT.

There is a concerning inconsistency between the main result and the ablation: the main MSRL result uses the 22k + 5.5k configuration (96.5/78.6/83.8), while Table 5 shows the 22k + 11k configuration is better (97.5/79.5/83.8). No justification is given for not using the stronger configuration as the main model.
The evaluation lacks variance estimates or significance tests, making small reported gains difficult to trust, especially given multiple decision points in data construction and reward design.
Important baselines are missing, including Qwen2.5-VL-72B and other recent large open-source MLLMs; chart-specific RL methods such as Chart-R1 or BigCharts-R1 are mentioned but not compared.

Potential benchmark contamination is not thoroughly ruled out: the training corpus is built from arXiv papers published in 2023 and earlier, while ChartMimic/ReachQA examples may also originate from similar sources.
The visual reward relies on an MLLM judge from the same family as the base model, raising concerns about evaluator bias and reward hacking; human correlation is checked on only 200 samples.
Reproducibility is limited: the 3M/33k datasets do not appear to be publicly released, and licensing/ethical issues around using arXiv tables and LLM-generated code are not discussed.

Some technical and clarity issues remain: reward weight notation is potentially confusing (e.g., w_t and w_e used in multiple senses), figure/table captions are inconsistent, and reference formatting has typos.

strengths: Constructs a large-scale chart-to-code training corpus (3M pairs) from real arXiv tables, substantially larger and more diverse than prior datasets, and uses it to systematically study SFT scaling behavior.
Identifies and empirically characterizes the SFT performance plateau, then proposes MSRL, a two-stage RL strategy with multi-granularity textual and visual rewards, to break it.
Achieves strong empirical results: new SOTA among open-source models on ChartMimic and ReachQA, competitive with GPT-4o on many metrics, with detailed low-level score breakdowns.
Provides comprehensive ablations: SFT vs. RL, reward design, GRPO vs. DPO, visual evaluator choices, dataset comparison, generalization to Seaborn/Plotly, and GPU-hour trade-offs.
Includes clear implementation details, prompts, and reproducibility statement in the appendix, making the training pipeline relatively transparent.
weaknesses: The proposed method is largely a combination of existing techniques (GRPO, rule-based reward, MLLM-as-judge visual reward, two-stage curriculum); the algorithmic novelty is moderate rather than fundamental.

There is an inconsistency in the two-stage RL setup: Appendix B states Stage 2 uses 11k pairs, while Section 4.3/Table 5 and the final MSRL results appear to use 5.5k pairs (50% of Stage 2 data). This undermines exact reproducibility of the reported configuration.
The dataset is a central contribution, but the paper does not clearly state that it will be publicly released; it promises code and prompts in the supplementary but not the full dataset.
Evaluation is limited to two chart-to-code benchmarks; there is no human evaluation of final rendered chart quality/readability, and no variance or error bars for the main results.
The visual reward relies on Qwen2.5-VL-72B, from the same model family as the 7B base model, raising potential reward-bias/reward-hacking concerns despite the appendix correlation analysis.

The SFT plateau conclusion is based on a single base model and one dataset; it is unclear whether the plateau generalizes across model scales, training schedules, or other structured generation tasks.
Benchmark decontamination is handled only by restricting training papers to 2023 and earlier for ChartMimic, with no exact ID-level decontamination reported for ReachQA or the final evaluation sets.
